correctness.rationale: Exact finite simple graph definition and power-observation process are specified. When at least one original vertex is selected, a chosen set is feasible if and only if the unobserved edge-subdivision graph on the unselected original labels is acyclic: every remaining cycle is a permanent forcing obstruction, while a forest can be leaf-peeled after selected-original incident subdivision nodes force all originals. Edge-count inequality gives lower bound n-2 and only two equality types; original-free sets below this size are excluded by the same cycle obstruction, with n=3 singleton edge case verified. The bijection maps each type-B optimum to a unique edge between two type-A Johnson vertices; local slides precisely join the midpoint to its two endpoints. Exact distance formulas for a subdivided graph prove all eccentricities and sharp radius/diameter, including n=3,4,5 boundaries. Included standalone scripts check full brute-force power domination through n=7 and an independent standard-library adjacency-set graph construction and simulation through n=6, with structural and metric checks through n=16. All tests passed from delivered source files. Finite tests support but do not substitute the all-order proof.

value.rationale: Power domination models low-budget network monitoring. Subdividing every link of a clique is a natural operation, but changes optimal sensor count to n-2, and creates two distinct optimizer types. Their adjacency-constrained migration graph is not merely connected: it is an exact edge-subdivision of Johnson J(n,2), giving canonical shortest migration routes and an exact diameter that stabilizes at six despite the growing underlying graph and budget. This precise structural realization provides an infinite-family benchmark for physically feasible optimal sensor migration and a nontrivial correspondence between propagation, forests, and reconfiguration geometry. The known OEIS count alone would not confer value; the additional classification and sharp metric do.
